ai,Claude,"Looked in the mirror (screenshots above — headless Chrome served the **dark** theme, which is the more distinctive of the two). Here's the review as the design lead, in the plugin's own terms.

**Strong concept, safe execution.** The site has a genuine thesis — *serif = the human voice, monospace = the machine* — which is exactly the kind of subject-true idea the plugin asks for. But the thesis is **stated, not performed**: it's carried by two *default* typefaces and diffused across six low-volume decorative systems, so nothing on the page is the one thing you'd remember. By the plugin's bar (""could not be mistaken for anyone else's; take one real risk""), this is a B+ — polished and considerate, but it hasn't spent its boldness anywhere.
- **The human/machine type *concept*** is the best asset. Don't discard it — amplify it.
- **Cobalt + amber** deliberately dodges the accent side of the AI-default palettes. Good, non-templated choice.
- **Numbered timeline** passes the ""structure encodes truth"" test — it's a real dated 11-week sequence, so `01…11` is earned, not decoration.
- Dark mode is genuinely handsome; quality floor (focus, reduced-motion, responsive) is met.

1. **The type has no personality.** That's Palatino/Book Antiqua (a system book-serif) + system mono. They're what *anyone* would reach for — so the ""human vs machine"" idea never actually *sings*, because both voices are generic. This is the single biggest lever.

2. **No signature / no hero thesis.** The masthead is the template answer: left title + italic lede + four pill ""facts."" Handsome, but there's no characteristic moment that embodies ""Information Age."" The graph-paper wash is the only candidate, and it's passive — and a mild AI tell in its own right (the ""technical grid"" look).
3. **Light mode brushes AI-default look #1** — warm cream (`#f6f3ec` ≈ the `#F4F1EA` cliché) under a serif display. Dark mode escapes it; light mode doesn't.
4. **Boldness is diffuse** — grid wash + cobalt chips + amber pills + gradient bars + mono labels + node rings all playing at the same mid volume. Chanel's mirror rule: *take one thing off.*
5. **Motion contributes nothing** — only a card-hover lift.

The move is to make the duality **the signature**, and give both voices real character. Crucially, since this is now a **local file, not an Artifact, the font-CDN block is gone** — real webfonts are back on the table, which unlocks #1.

**Signature — the ""decode"" masthead.** On load, the title arrives as **monospace machine-text and resolves into a characterful serif** over ~900ms — literally enacting the course's promise (raw input → fluent, capable human). Reduced-motion shows the resolved state. This is the hero-as-thesis, and everything else stays quiet around it.

**Restraint:** retire the full-page graph-paper; let the grid exist **only behind the hero**, as the field the title resolves across, then clear. That's the ""one accessory removed.""

Becoming a thoughtful, capable, and ethical participant in a digital and AI‑saturated world.
Computing, technology, and artificial intelligence now shape how we learn, work, communicate, and make decisions. This course helps you meet that world on your own terms.

Across the term you'll use computing as a tool to work and create with data; learn effectively — with and without AI; find and judge digital information; reason about the ethics of technology; and build a professional digital presence for your career. It's designed for students of every background, and assumes no prior experience.

Each week centers on a short discussion — a post and a reply that connect the week's ideas to real situations — and the term builds toward three hands-on assignments. There are no exams; you learn by making, evaluating, and reflecting.

GOAL 01

Work and create with data using everyday computing tools.

GOAL 02

Learn effectively and think critically — with and without AI.

GOAL 03

Find, evaluate, and use digital information responsibly.

GOAL 04

Reason about the ethics, privacy, and power of technology.

GOAL 05

Build a professional digital presence for your career.
Discussions are the graded weekly posts-and-replies; Participation covers live engagement, attendance, and the Week 1 tool survey. Your lowest one or two discussion scores are dropped.

Three projects carry most of your grade — each turns a stretch of the course into something you make. They're listed in the order they come due.

Choose a real-world claim or trending topic and evaluate the credibility of several sources that make claims about it. Trace where the information comes from, apply a source-evaluation framework, and reach an evidence-based judgment about what can and cannot be trusted.
• A 900–1200 word report evaluating at least 4 sources — a news outlet, a social/UGC source, and one AI-generated answer
• A completed SIFT or CRAAP source-evaluation table for each source
• A ""trace the origin"" section identifying an original claim and one instance of bias, misinformation, or an unverifiable AI claim
• A short reflection on how your own assumptions and search habits shaped what you found
AssessesLateral reading · evidence vs. opinion · spotting bias & misinformation · critical assessment of AI output · cited reasoning

Design and publish a cohesive professional online presence that represents you intentionally to employers, collaborators, and academic contacts — then reflect on how your choices serve your audience, privacy, and personal brand.
• A published, public-facing profile: a complete LinkedIn profile or a personal website / portfolio page
• At least two showcased items — projects, coursework, or experiences — aimed at a target audience
• A privacy & digital-footprint audit with at least two concrete changes made
• A 400–600 word reflection on audience, brand choices, and balancing openness with privacy
AssessesProfessional self-presentation · audience-aware communication · web/profile tools · privacy management · reflective self-assessment

Your capstone brings the term together: take a real dataset, clean and analyze it, and produce a data-driven story that communicates a clear insight to a non-technical audience — integrating computational thinking, visualization, and narrative. You have two weeks for this final project.
• A cleaned dataset (from open data or provided options) with a documented question and your cleaning steps
• At least two clear, well-labeled visualizations that support your main insight
• A 700–1000 word data story or short deck presenting question, findings, visuals, and one actionable takeaway
• A brief methods-and-limitations note covering sources, assumptions, ethics, and responsible AI use
AssessesProblem decomposition · working with structured data · chart selection · data ethics & limitations · communicating insight to a general audience
Using AI in this course AI POLICY
AI tools are welcome here — this is a course about using them well. Use them to brainstorm, explain, and get unstuck, but the thinking and the final work must be yours.
When AI meaningfully shaped a submission, say so and how. Always verify what it tells you against a real source — confident wrong answers are the norm, not the exception.
Submit your own work, cite the sources and tools you rely on, and don't misrepresent others' words or data as your own. When in doubt about what's allowed, ask first — it's always the safe move.

Everyone deserves an equal path through this course. If any material or activity creates a barrier, reach out early and we'll arrange accommodations together, in coordination with disability services.

Discussions build a shared conversation, so they're due weekly — but your lowest one or two scores are dropped for the times life gets in the way. For assignments, reach out ahead of the due date if you need flexibility.
Questions, office hours, meeting details, and instructor contact live on the course portal. No question is too basic — this course assumes no prior experience, and asking is how the class works.
Topics, readings, and dates may shift as the term unfolds. The online schedule is always the source of truth — check it regularly for the current version.

Becoming a thoughtful, capable, and ethical participant in a digital and AI‑saturated world.
Computing, technology, and artificial intelligence now shape how we learn, work, communicate, and make decisions. This course helps you meet that world on your own terms.

Across the term you'll use computing as a tool to work and create with data; learn effectively — with and without AI; find and judge digital information; reason about the ethics of technology; and build a professional digital presence for your career. It's designed for students of every background, and assumes no prior experience.

Each week centers on a short discussion — a post and a reply that connect the week's ideas to real situations — and the term builds toward three hands-on assignments. There are no exams; you learn by making, evaluating, and reflecting.

GOAL 01

Work and create with data using everyday computing tools.

GOAL 02

Learn effectively and think critically — with and without AI.

GOAL 03

Find, evaluate, and use digital information responsibly.

GOAL 04

Reason about the ethics, privacy, and power of technology.

GOAL 05

Build a professional digital presence for your career.
Discussions are the graded weekly posts-and-replies; Participation covers live engagement, attendance, and the Week 1 tool survey. Your lowest one or two discussion scores are dropped.

Becoming a thoughtful, capable, and ethical participant in a digital and AI‑saturated world.
Computing, technology, and artificial intelligence now shape how we learn, work, communicate, and make decisions. This course helps you meet that world on your own terms.

Across the term you'll use computing as a tool to work and create with data; learn effectively — with and without AI; find and judge digital information; reason about the ethics of technology; and build a professional digital presence for your career. It's designed for students of every background, and assumes no prior experience.

Each week centers on a short discussion — a post and a reply that connect the week's ideas to real situations — and the term builds toward three hands-on assignments. There are no exams; you learn by making, evaluating, and reflecting.

GOAL 01

Work and create with data using everyday computing tools.

GOAL 02

Learn effectively and think critically — with and without AI.

GOAL 03

Find, evaluate, and use digital information responsibly.

GOAL 04

Reason about the ethics, privacy, and power of technology.

GOAL 05

Build a professional digital presence for your career.
Discussions are the graded weekly posts-and-replies; Participation covers live engagement, attendance, and the Week 1 tool survey. Your lowest one or two discussion scores are dropped.

Technology and AI are rewriting what it means to be a capable learner — this week you'll map that new landscape and find your place in it.
• Describe how digital tools and AI are reshaping how we learn, work, and make decisions
• Set personal goals for building your computer and AI skills this term
• Identify your current strengths and gaps as a digital learner — without judgment
• Navigate the core tools and habits you'll use throughout this course
• 2025 EDUCAUSE Horizon Report · EDUCAUSEThe annual scan of how AI and emerging tech are reshaping teaching and learning.
• Guidance for Generative AI in Education · UNESCO, 2023Global policy framing for how learners should adapt to generative AI.
Digital literacyAI-saturated worldSelf-directed learningGrowth mindset
WhyWhatever your field, the ability to keep learning with new tools will shape your career more than any single skill you memorize.
There are science-backed ways to learn faster and remember longer — and once you know them, every future class gets easier.
• Apply evidence-based techniques like spaced practice and retrieval to your coursework
• Explain how memory and attention work well enough to study smarter, not harder
• Use AI tools to support learning without letting them do the thinking for you
• Design a realistic weekly study plan that fits your life
• Learning How to Learn · Oakley & Sejnowski · CourseraThe world's most popular MOOC on evidence-based study strategies — free to audit.
• Free full course videos · Barbara OakleyOpenly hosted videos for direct, no-signup access to the core techniques.
Spaced repetitionRetrieval practiceMetacognitionCognitive load
WhyMastering how you learn pays off in every course, job training, and skill you'll ever pick up.
From email to shared docs to group chats, most work today happens online — this week you'll learn to communicate clearly and collaborate smoothly in digital spaces.
• Write clear, professional messages appropriate to email, chat, and other channels
• Collaborate effectively using shared documents and cloud-based tools
• Apply good etiquette and norms for online teamwork and discussion
• Choose the right communication tool for a given audience and purpose
• The Core Rules of Netiquette · Virginia SheaA concise, classic set of principles for respectful online communication.
• Atlassian Team Playbook · AtlassianFree, practical ""Plays"" for real-world team collaboration, including async work.
Netiquette & toneSync vs. asyncCloud collaborationAudience awareness
WhyEmployers consistently rank clear digital communication among the top skills they look for.
In a world flooded with content, knowing how to find and trust the right information is a genuine superpower.
• Search effectively to find relevant, high-quality information
• Evaluate sources for credibility, bias, and accuracy
• Recognize misinformation, manipulation, and common online red flags
• Cite and use information ethically and responsibly
• SIFT: The Four Moves · Mike CaulfieldThe widely adopted Stop–Investigate–Find–Trace method for fast source evaluation.
• Web Literacy for Student Fact-Checkers · Open textbookA free book teaching lateral reading and practical fact-checking skills.
Lateral readingMis / disinformationBias & credibilityCitation
WhyEvery big decision — health, money, your vote, your studies — depends on telling reliable information from noise.
AI tools are everywhere now — this week you'll learn what they actually do, where they shine, and where they quietly go wrong.
• Explain in plain language how generative AI and large language models work
• Write effective prompts to get useful results from AI tools
• Recognize AI limitations like hallucination, bias, and confident wrong answers
• Use AI responsibly and transparently in your studies and work
• Elements of AI · University of HelsinkiA free, non-technical intro to what AI is and isn't — taken by a million+ learners.
• AI Competency Framework for Students · UNESCO, 2024An international reference for the AI competencies students should develop.
Generative AI & LLMsPromptingHallucinationHuman verification
WhyKnowing how to use AI well — and when not to trust it — is becoming as essential as knowing how to use the internet.
Ethics, Privacy & Power in an AI Age
Behind every app and algorithm are real choices about privacy, fairness, and power — this week you'll learn to see and question them.
• Analyze the ethical trade-offs built into everyday technologies and AI systems
• Explain how your personal data is collected, used, and monetized
• Identify how algorithms can amplify bias or concentrate power
• Make more informed choices to protect your own privacy
• Ethics of AI · University of HelsinkiA free course on fairness, accountability, transparency, and human rights in AI.
• Surveillance Self-Defense · EFFA practical, reputable guide to protecting your privacy and understanding data surveillance.
Privacy & surveillanceAlgorithmic biasPower & accountabilityConsent
WhyThe technologies you use every day make decisions about you — understanding the ethics helps you protect yourself.
Great technology starts with people, not gadgets — this week you'll learn to design solutions around real human needs.
• Describe the core stages of a human-centered design process
• Use empathy and user research to understand a problem before solving it
• Prototype and test simple solutions and gather feedback
• Evaluate whether a technology genuinely serves the people who use it
• The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design · IDEO.orgA free guide through the Inspiration–Ideation–Implementation process.
• Design Thinking Resources · Stanford d.schoolA free toolkit of design-thinking methods and mindsets.
Empathy & user researchDesign thinkingPrototypingAccessibility
WhyWhether you build products or lead a team, designing around real human needs is what makes your work useful.
Your online presence is often the first impression you make — this week you'll learn to shape it intentionally and professionally.
• Build or refine a professional profile such as a resume or LinkedIn page
• Manage your digital footprint and privacy across public platforms
• Present your skills and experiences authentically to different audiences
• Understand how employers and others evaluate you online
• Your Digital Footprint · University of YorkPractical guidance on curating a positive, professional online presence.
• Digital Identity & E-professionalism · Manchester MetOn balancing personal vs. professional online personas.
Digital footprintPersonal brandingNetworkingReputation
WhyRecruiters and collaborators will look you up — a thoughtful presence opens doors a careless one can close.
Data is the raw material of the digital age — this week you'll learn to collect, organize, and make sense of it using everyday tools.
• Organize and clean data using spreadsheets and basic tools
• Perform simple calculations, sorting, and filtering to answer questions
• Interpret basic statistics and spot patterns responsibly
• Recognize common data errors and misleading numbers
• Data Feminism · D'Ignazio & Klein · MIT PressA free, full-text book on thinking critically about data, bias, and power.
• Google Data Analytics · Google · CourseraA free-to-audit, hands-on intro to collecting, cleaning, and analyzing real data.
Structured dataData cleaningDescriptive statsData quality
WhyFrom budgets to research, working with data lets you back up your ideas with evidence in almost any job.
Numbers alone rarely persuade — this week you'll learn to turn data into clear, honest visuals and stories that people remember.

Three projects carry most of your grade — each turns a stretch of the course into something you make. They're listed in the order they come due.

Choose a real-world claim or trending topic and evaluate the credibility of several sources that make claims about it. Trace where the information comes from, apply a source-evaluation framework, and reach an evidence-based judgment about what can and cannot be trusted.
• A 900–1200 word report evaluating at least 4 sources — a news outlet, a social/UGC source, and one AI-generated answer
• A completed SIFT or CRAAP source-evaluation table for each source
• A ""trace the origin"" section identifying an original claim and one instance of bias, misinformation, or an unverifiable AI claim
• A short reflection on how your own assumptions and search habits shaped what you found
AssessesLateral reading · evidence vs. opinion · spotting bias & misinformation · critical assessment of AI output · cited reasoning

Design and publish a cohesive professional online presence that represents you intentionally to employers, collaborators, and academic contacts — then reflect on how your choices serve your audience, privacy, and personal brand.
• A published, public-facing profile: a complete LinkedIn profile or a personal website / portfolio page
• At least two showcased items — projects, coursework, or experiences — aimed at a target audience
• A privacy & digital-footprint audit with at least two concrete changes made
• A 400–600 word reflection on audience, brand choices, and balancing openness with privacy
AssessesProfessional self-presentation · audience-aware communication · web/profile tools · privacy management · reflective self-assessment

Your capstone brings the term together: take a real dataset, clean and analyze it, and produce a data-driven story that communicates a clear insight to a non-technical audience — integrating computational thinking, visualization, and narrative. You have two weeks for this final project.
• A cleaned dataset (from open data or provided options) with a documented question and your cleaning steps
• At least two clear, well-labeled visualizations that support your main insight
• A 700–1000 word data story or short deck presenting question, findings, visuals, and one actionable takeaway
• A brief methods-and-limitations note covering sources, assumptions, ethics, and responsible AI use
AssessesProblem decomposition · working with structured data · chart selection · data ethics & limitations · communicating insight to a general audience
Using AI in this course AI POLICY
AI tools are welcome here — this is a course about using them well. Use them to brainstorm, explain, and get unstuck, but the thinking and the final work must be yours.
When AI meaningfully shaped a submission, say so and how. Always verify what it tells you against a real source — confident wrong answers are the norm, not the exception.
Submit your own work, cite the sources and tools you rely on, and don't misrepresent others' words or data as your own. When in doubt about what's allowed, ask first — it's always the safe move.

Everyone deserves an equal path through this course. If any material or activity creates a barrier, reach out early and we'll arrange accommodations together, in coordination with disability services.

Discussions build a shared conversation, so they're due weekly — but your lowest one or two scores are dropped for the times life gets in the way. For assignments, reach out ahead of the due date if you need flexibility.
Questions, office hours, meeting details, and instructor contact live on the course portal. No question is too basic — this course assumes no prior experience, and asking is how the class works.
Topics, readings, and dates may shift as the term unfolds. The online schedule is always the source of truth — check it regularly for the current version.

column1: ai,Tool:Agent,"[Agent spawned: general-purpose] Front-end code and a11y audit
Prompt: You are a senior front-end engineer doing a code-quality and accessibility audit of a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS + a small vanilla-JS script). Read it:

Context: it's a university course syllabus rendered as a single-file TABBED app. A sticky `<nav class=""tabs"">` holds four `<a class=""tab"" href=""#start"">`-style links plus a `<button class=""viewall-btn"">`. A small script at the bottom adds a `js` class to the root, toggles `.is-active` on `.view` divs based on `location.hash` (with a `hashchange` listener), sets `aria-current=""page""` on the active tab, and toggles a `showall` class for a ""view all / print"" mode. There is a no-JS fallback (all views visible) and `@media print` rules. Type is system-serif + monospace; there are light/dark themes via CSS custom properties and `prefers-color-scheme` + `[data-theme]` overrides.
Audit rigorously and report CONCRETE issues with file locations/quotes and fixes, grouped by severity:

1. **Accessibility**: Are the ""tabs"" semantically correct (they're anchor links switching views — is ARIA tab pattern expected, or is link+aria-current acceptable)? Do hidden (`display:none`) views correctly remove content from the a11y tree and tab order? Keyboard operability of the view-all button (`aria-pressed` present?), focus management when switching views, focus-visible, color-contrast risks (esp. the `.tba` amber chips, mono labels at small sizes, dark theme), the decorative graph-paper background, motion/reduced-motion, heading order (h1→h2→h3), landmark structure, link `target=""_blank""` + `rel`.

2. **JS robustness**: hash-routing edge cases (unknown/empty hash, an in-content anchor that isn't a view, back/forward behavior, the `showall` + hashchange interaction, `scrollIntoView` argument correctness `reduce ? true : {…}`), any failure if elements are missing.

3. **CSS/structure**: selector-specificity collisions, spacing systems that could double/collapse, sticky-nav stacking/overlap or z-index issues, responsive breakpoints, print correctness, anything brittle.
4. **General robustness / future-proofing**: what would break first if content grew, and the top 5 highest-leverage fixes ranked.

Becoming a thoughtful, capable, and ethical participant in a digital and AI‑saturated world.
Computing, technology, and artificial intelligence now shape how we learn, work, communicate, and make decisions. This course helps you meet that world on your own terms.

Across the term you'll use computing as a tool to work and create with data; learn effectively — with and without AI; find and judge digital information; reason about the ethics of technology; and build a professional digital presence for your career. It's designed for students of every background, and assumes no prior experience.

Each week centers on a short discussion — a post and a reply that connect the week's ideas to real situations — and the term builds toward three hands-on assignments. There are no exams; you learn by making, evaluating, and reflecting.

GOAL 01

Work and create with data using everyday computing tools.

GOAL 02

Learn effectively and think critically — with and without AI.

GOAL 03

Find, evaluate, and use digital information responsibly.

GOAL 04

Reason about the ethics, privacy, and power of technology.

GOAL 05

Build a professional digital presence for your career.
Discussions are the graded weekly posts-and-replies; Participation covers live engagement, attendance, and the Week 1 tool survey. Your lowest one or two discussion scores are dropped.

AI tools are welcome here — this is a course about using them well. Use them to brainstorm, explain, and get unstuck, but the thinking and the final work must be yours.
When AI meaningfully shaped a submission, say so and how. Always verify what it tells you against a real source — confident wrong answers are the norm, not the exception.
Submit your own work, cite the sources and tools you rely on, and don't misrepresent others' words or data as your own. When in doubt about what's allowed, ask first — it's always the safe move.

Only the container changed — 4 tabbed views (Start here / Schedule / Assignments / Policies), slim A1–A3 markers left in the timeline as links to the Assignments view, a ""What you'll need"" logistics panel, and a ""View all / Print"" button that reflows everything into one document.
## 1. Assignment cards pulled out of the timeline — help or hurt alignment?
**Mild net hurt for the week→assignment story, partially offset.**

- **Preserved:** the temporal cue survives — the A1 marker still sits after Week 4, A2 after Week 8, A3 after Week 11 (`<div class=""ms-inline"">` in-place). A student still sees *when* each assignment lands relative to which weeks.

- **Lost:** the *substance* of the mapping. Previously the full card — deliverables **and** the ""Assesses"" line — sat directly under the feeding weeks. Now the timeline shows only `Assignment 1 · Source Investigation · See details →`; the skills mapping lives one click away in a separate tab. The week → assignment → skill chain is now split across two views.

- **Weak landing:** markers link to `#assignments` (the whole view), not to a specific card — no per-assignment anchor, scroll, or highlight. Clicking the A2 marker dumps you at the top of a 3-card list.

- **One-directional and mapless:** the Assignments view never says which weeks feed each project (""Assessed skills"" is listed, but not ""Builds on Weeks 9–11""). So from the assignments side the alignment story is *invisible* — the capstone doesn't reveal that it draws on Weeks 9–11 plus ethics from 5/6.

- **Offsetting gain:** consolidating the three cards lets a student compare scope, weight, and the make-arc (source eval → digital presence → data story) side by side — a synthesis the old scattered layout lacked. `View all / Print` fully restores linear adjacency.
## 2. New issues introduced by the tab reorganization
- **Curriculum discoverability dropped.** Empty hash defaults to ""Start here""; the entire 11-week arc and all deliverables are now behind tabs. A quick visitor may never see the actual course.
